title: Enhanced Air Cargo Advance Screening (ACAS)
summary:
The Department of Homeland Security just tightened advance screening for air cargo bound for the United States. U.S. Customs and Border Protection will now require more information about shipments before they are loaded on planes, aiming to spot and stop high‑risk cargo earlier. The rule takes effect immediately, with a 12‑month period of restrained enforcement while companies adapt, and public comments are open through January 20, 2026.

What’s changing? In addition to the basics, shippers must provide the receiver’s email and phone, where the goods were packed or will be picked up, and who will physically receive them. If the shipper is not vetted through a government‑recognized “known consignor” program, extra details kick in: the shipper’s contact info, the customer’s account information with the logistics provider (such as account name, issuer, number, how often they ship, when the account was created, and how they pay), and in some cases the device addresses used to create the account, start the shipment, or file the data. For walk‑in shipments or personal effects, staff must record text from a government photo ID, and CBP may require a copy to be kept for three years with prior notice. For online marketplace purchases, filers may need a link or item code plus the buyer’s device address. All data must be sent before loading. Customs and Border Protection says it will treat this information as confidential and is updating its privacy materials.

Who stands to benefit? Passengers, crews, airports, and nearby communities, because authorities can identify suspicious cargo earlier, issue do‑not‑load instructions when needed, and focus screening where it matters most. Legitimate shippers may also see fewer disruptions over time as better data helps clear low‑risk packages faster. The rule could indirectly help curb illegal goods, including synthetic drugs shipped by air.

Who may feel the strain? Airlines, freight forwarders, brokers, software vendors, and online marketplaces will likely shoulder new data collection, system upgrades, and training. Some companies—especially smaller firms and foreign operators with different processes—may face short‑term delays as they adjust. There are privacy concerns about collecting device addresses and keeping ID copies, even with promised safeguards. The government estimates compliance costs at roughly $117–$119 million per year over ten years; benefits are not easily quantified but are framed around avoiding rare, high‑impact events. Enforcement will be phased in for 12 months for companies making good‑faith progress, but willful violations can still draw penalties.

If your business touches cross‑border air cargo, now is the time to map your data flows, engage your IT and compliance teams, talk to partners and platforms about what’s needed, and consider submitting feedback on the rule at regulations.gov.
